Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

similar adjective

also alike, similar to, very similar, as like as two peas, resemble, in a similar vein, take after

classical

Cic. Sen. 80: nihil esse mortī tam simile quam somnum
Ter. Ad. 411: est similis majōrum suum

similis, simile

adjective, third declension; with the genitive or the dative · Declension on Wiktionary

similar, like

What a thing is like goes in the genitive in Plautus and Terence (tuī similis, like you); Cicero keeps the genitive for persons and uses the dative for things, and after Augustus the dative is usual (Lewis & Short). Alike, of two or more, is inter sē similēs; the opposite is dissimilis (see different).

Other words

  • persimilis, persimile — very similar, very like

    adjective, third declension · also used · classical · Cic. Pis. 93: statuam istīus persimilem (Lewis & Short); Hor. Ars 6–7 (Lewis & Short) · Declension on Wiktionary

  • cōnsimilis, cōnsimile — just like, similar in every way

    adjective, third declension · also used · classical · Caes. BG 2.11 (Lewis & Short); Cic. de Or. 1.149 (Lewis & Short) · Declension on Wiktionary

    Most frequent in Plautus, Terence and Lucretius (Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • neque aqua aquae nec lacte est lactis, crēde mī, usquam similius, quam hic tuī est, tūque hujus autem

    water is not more like water, nor milk more like milk, believe me, than he is like you and you like himPlaut. Men. 1089–1090

  • jam vērō vidētis nihil esse mortī tam simile quam somnum

    and you see that nothing is so like death as sleepCic. Sen. 80

  • incidī in māteriam vēram sed simillimam fictae

    I have come upon a story that is true, but very like a made-up onePlin. Ep. 9.33.1

  • Ad similem sententiam.

    In a similar vein.Traupman 110

  • similis esse (+ gen.)

    to take afterTraupman 389

See also same, different.
